lesson.title: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps
lesson.subtitle: Ten risks, and why model output is untrusted

video.title: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps

scenes.visual: Cards: Library chatbot; Its instructions; A database password.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A library chatbot leaked its own password. A student asked it to repeat its instructions, and there, inside them, was the database password. The developer had put it there to save time.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps
scenes.narration: Today: ten risks in apps built on language models, and a defence for each.

scenes.visual: Cards: OWASP 2025: ten risks; What goes in; What comes out; The system around.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: OWASP is a non-profit community that publishes free security guidance. Its 2025 list for language-model apps has ten risks. Let's take them in three groups: what goes in, what comes out, and the system around them.

scenes.visual: An architecture: the user's prompt, the training data and the retrieval store all flow into the model, which writes the reply; each way in lights up as its risk is named (01, 04, 08).
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: What goes in. Number one, prompt injection: instructions hidden in input steer the model. Number four, data and model poisoning: bad training data plants wrong behaviour. Number eight, vector and embedding weaknesses: a retrieval store that mixes users' documents, or accepts poisoned ones.

scenes.visual: A list: 02 Sensitive information disclosure; 07 System prompt leakage; 05 Improper output handling; 09 Misinformation.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: What comes out. Number two, sensitive information disclosure: it reveals personal data or secrets. Number seven, system prompt leakage, like our library bot. Number five, improper output handling: its reply is pasted into a page, a query or a command, and runs. Number nine, misinformation: confident, wrong answers people act on.

scenes.visual: A list: 03 Supply chain; 06 Excessive agency; 10 Unbounded consumption.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Finally, the system around them. Number three, the supply chain: models, data and plug-ins made by others. Number six, excessive agency: more tools and permissions than the job needs. Number ten, unbounded consumption: one user's flood of requests runs up the bill, or takes it down.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A chatbot's reply is pasted straight into the course web page, and one reply contains a piece of script. Which risk is that?

scenes.visual: Two columns. Don't: Paste it into HTML; Build SQL from it. Do: Escape it first; Query parameters; Never into a shell.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Improper output handling. The model's reply is text from a source you don't control. So treat it like any user input: escape it before HTML, use parameters for SQL, never pass it to a shell.

scenes.visual: A code card: escaping in the wrong order prints &lt;b>; the ampersand line moves to the top and it prints <b>.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Escaping turns special characters into harmless codes, so the browser shows them instead of running them. Do it in the wrong order, and you escape your own escapes: the page shows a mess. The ampersand must go first.

scenes.visual: A list: No secrets in the system prompt; Keys stay in the app; Only this user's data; Check replies before they go out.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: And the library bot? Never put secrets in a system prompt: assume it will be read. Keep keys in the app, give the model only this user's data, and check replies before they go out.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Trained on a private line; It repeats a card number; Privacy noise; Less useful.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: a model that remembers
scenes.narration: In the app, a tiny model has memorised a private line from its training data. Ask it the right way and it repeats a card number. Add privacy noise and watch the leak close, and the usefulness drop.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A study assistant can delete files, but its job is only to read them. Which risk is that?

scenes.visual: The summary: Ten risks: in, out, the system; Output is untrusted input; No secrets in prompts; The fewest tools. Takeaway: Assume the model will be tricked; design so it doesn't matter.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ten risks · Untrusted output · No secrets · Fewest tools
scenes.narration: Excessive agency: take the delete tool away. Remember: ten risks in three groups, model output is untrusted input, no secrets in prompts, and the fewest tools the job needs.

scenes.visual: A list: Go down the ten; Here? What stops it?; Fix the fastest three.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: go down the ten for an LLM app you use or are building. For each, write one line: could it happen here, and what stops it? Then fix the fastest three.

checkpoints.prompt: A chatbot's reply is pasted straight into the course web page, and one reply contains a piece of script. Which risk is that?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: the reply was used without being checked, so the browser ran it. Treat model output as untrusted input.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the problem is what the page did with the reply. That's improper output handling.

checkpoints.prompt: A study assistant can delete files, but its job is only to read them. Which risk is that?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: it holds a power its job doesn't need. Take the delete tool away.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the problem is a tool it doesn't need. That's excessive agency.
